title: The search
hookLine: the search fails; Sampati gives his dead brother water, then sees Sita
carry: tarpan: the dead are remembered with water
last: CHATURMAS: WAITING IS A SACRED SEASON.

lines: A NAME THAT STOPS A ROOM.
cards: Some names stop a room. Say a grandparent's name at a family dinner, and somebody goes quiet. Hold on to that.

The rains end, and Sugriva, now king and comfortable, has half forgotten his promise. Lakshmana storms into the monkey city so angry the walls seem to shake, and it takes Tara, the wise queen, to calm him down.
Then Sugriva moves fast. He sends his whole army out in four great search parties: north, east, west and south. One month, he says.
Search every mountain, every forest, every cave. And he gives Hanuman, heading south, Rama's ring.

teach.b: The northern, eastern and western parties come home with nothing. The southern party, with Hanuman and young Angada, Vali's son, gets lost in an enchanted cave, and the month runs out.
They sit down on the shore at the very tip of the land, sure they've failed and afraid to go home empty-handed.
As they talk, Angada says one name: Jatayu, the old bird who died fighting Ravana. And a voice answers from the cliffs. An ancient vulture with no wings: Sampati, Jatayu's older brother.
Long ago, he says, the two of them raced toward the sun, and he spread his wings over his little brother, and his own wings burned away. He hadn't known Jatayu was dead.
And before he tells them anything else, he asks for one thing: carry me down to the sea, so I can offer water for my brother. They do. Then the old bird gives them what a whole army couldn't find.
I can see her, he says.
Across the ocean, in Lanka, sits Sita.
That water has a name in Hindu homes: tarpan. When someone dies, families offer water, often with a few sesame seeds, and say the person's name.
They do it in the rites after a death, on the yearly anniversary, and every year in Pitru Paksha, the fortnight of the ancestors. The teaching under it: the dead aren't erased.
They're still family, still named, still given something. And the answer arrived because someone spoke a dead bird's name with love.

how: Tarpan, offering water (often with sesame) while naming those who have died, is part of Hindu rites after a death, of yearly anniversaries, and of Pitru Paksha, the fortnight for the ancestors. The Sampati scene leads straight into the Sundara Kanda, Hanuman's leap to Lanka, which is often recited on its own.

games.q: you're Sampati. strangers have just told you your little brother died fighting Ravana, and they need your news fast. what do you do first?
o: tell them where Sita is, and grieve later.
ask them to carry you to the sea to offer water for him.

games.why: in Valmiki, he asks for the water first. then he tells them he can see Sita, across the sea in Lanka.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've lost: a grandparent, a friend, even a pet. If you keep a shrine, or just have a glass of water nearby, pour a little slowly and say their name out loud.
If not, simply say the name, and one thing they gave you that you still carry. You don't have to make yourself sad. You're keeping them in the family, the way Sampati did.

wordCard.voice: The search. An army in four directions, a month gone, and the answer from a wingless old bird who first stopped to give his brother water.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tarpana, 'satisfying, refreshing': water offered to the gods, the sages and the ancestors.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: tarpan, the dead are remembered with water. Sampati gave his first. Day fifty-seven.
